title: Maximum Number of Pairs in Array
description:
# Maximum Number of Pairs in Array

Given an integer array `nums`, repeatedly choose two unused elements with the same value and form a pair. Return an array `[pairs, leftovers]`:

* `pairs` is the maximum number of equal-value pairs that can be formed.
* `leftovers` is the number of elements not used in any pair.

## Example 1:

**Input:** nums = [1,3,2,1,3,2,2]

**Output:** [3,1]

**Explanation:** The pairs are `(1,1)`, `(3,3)`, and one pair of `2`s. One `2` is left over.

## Example 2:

**Input:** nums = [1,1]

**Output:** [1,0]

**Explanation:** Both elements form one pair, so no element is left over.

## Constraints:

* `0 <= nums.length <= 100`
* `0 <= nums[i] <= 100`

solutions.name: Bounded Frequency Array
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use the constraint `0 <= nums[i] <= 100` to allocate a frequency array of length `101`. Count each value, then add `count / 2` to the pair total and `count % 2` to the leftover total.

## Key Insight

Pairs depend only on how many times each value appears, not on where those values appear. The small value range lets us replace a hash table with direct indexing.

## Complexity Analysis

Let `U = 101` be the fixed value range. Counting takes O(n) time and scanning the range takes O(U) time. The frequency array uses O(U) space.

solutions.name: HashMap Frequency Counts
solutions.description:
## Approach

Count values in a `HashMap`, then apply the same frequency formula to every map entry. This works even if the value range were not small.

## Key Insight

The formula `pairs += count / 2` and `leftovers += count % 2` is the core of the problem. A hash map keeps that idea independent of the numeric bounds.

## Complexity Analysis

The expected time complexity is O(n), where `n` is the array length. The map stores `k` distinct values, so the extra space is O(k).

solutions.name: Toggle Set of Waiting Singles
solutions.description:
## Approach

Maintain a set of values that currently have one unpaired occurrence waiting. When a value is not in the set, add it. When it is already waiting, remove it and form one pair.

## Key Insight

Only parity matters for leftovers: after every two equal values, one pair is complete and no copy of that value is waiting. The final set size is the number of leftover elements.

## Complexity Analysis

The expected time complexity is O(n). The set stores at most one waiting copy per distinct value, so the extra space is O(k).

solutions.name: Sort Adjacent Equal Values
solutions.description:
## Approach

Sort the array so equal values are adjacent. Scan from left to right: if the current value equals the next value, consume both as one pair; otherwise, count the current value as leftover.

## Key Insight

Sorting turns the task of finding equal partners into a local adjacent comparison. It is slower than counting here, but it is a useful baseline when hash structures are unavailable.

## Complexity Analysis

Sorting dominates with O(n log n) time. The scan is O(n). Extra space depends on the sorting implementation; ignoring sort internals, the scan uses O(1) space.

solutions.name: Bounded Parity Table
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use a boolean array indexed by value to record whether one unmatched copy of that value is waiting. Each time a value appears, flip its waiting state. If it was already waiting, closing the pair increments the pair count.

## Key Insight

For this problem, the exact frequency is not always necessary while streaming. The parity of each value tells whether the next occurrence will create a pair or become a leftover candidate.

## Complexity Analysis

The array is scanned once, so the time complexity is O(n). The boolean table has one slot for each possible value, so the extra space is O(U), with `U = 101` under the constraints.
